proofs.proof_tex:
Write \(K_a=K_a(n_T)\), \(J_a=K_a(k_T)\), and
\[
 \sigma_{a,T}^2=\operatorname{Var}_P(X_{a,1}^{\Delta}),
 \qquad
 Z_T=(M_{1,\Delta}-PM_{1,\Delta})-(M_{0,\Delta}-PM_{0,\Delta}),
\]
\[
 C_T=(U_{1,\Delta}-PU_{1,\Delta})-(U_{0,\Delta}-PU_{0,\Delta}).
\]
By \(\mathrm{lem:arm\text{-}tape\text{-}equivalence}\), these are functions of deterministic prefixes of independent, identically distributed arm tapes.  By \(\mathrm{lem:old\text{-}cohort\text{-}correction}\), on \(E_T\),
\[
 \widehat\tau_{T,\Delta}-\tau+b_{T,\Delta}=Z_T+C_T. \tag{1}
\]
This is an unconditional identity in the tape variables; \(E_T\) only determines whether the observable estimator uses those prefixes.

First note that the delay envelope rules out infinite delays.  For each arm, continuity from above and \(\beta>0\) give
\[
 P\{D(a)=\infty\}=\lim_{u\to\infty}P\{D(a)>u\}
 \leq \lim_{u\to\infty}L(1+u)^{-\beta}=0. \tag{2}
\]
We next verify measurability.  On \(E_T\), the first \(K_a\) assignments to arm \(a\) occur no later than \(n_T\), and hence their ages at \(H_T\) are at least
\[
 H_T-n_T=m_T+\Delta_T=g_{T,\Delta}.
\]
The first \(J_a\) assignments occur no later than \(k_T\), and their ages are at least
\[
 H_T-k_T=h_{T,\Delta}.
\]
If one of these responses is revealed, \(O_{T,\Delta}\) records its outcome, delay, and revelation time.  If it is absent at \(H_T\), its delay exceeds the applicable guaranteed age, so its contribution to the corresponding truncated variable is known to be zero.  Thus every \(X_{a,j}^{\Delta}\), \(R_{a,j}^{\Delta}\), sample variance, gate, and endpoint is \(O_{T,\Delta}\)-measurable on \(E_T\).  The definitions on \(E_T^c\) are functions of the observed assignment counts, so the complete interval is measurable.

We establish a finite-sample guarantee for the concentration branch.  If \(X\in[-1,1]\), convexity of the exponential on this interval, followed by centering, gives
\[
 P\exp\{\lambda(X-PX)\}\leq \exp(\lambda^2/2).
\]
Multiplication over the independent tape variables, exponential Markov inequality, and optimization over \(\lambda\) yield
\[
 P\{|Z_T|>\sqrt{2S_Tx}\}\leq 2e^{-x},
 \qquad S_T=K_1^{-1}+K_0^{-1}. \tag{3}
\]
For \(R=Y\mathbf 1\{g_{T,\Delta}<D\leq h_{T,\Delta}\}\), bounded outcomes and the delay envelope imply
\[
 |R-PR|\leq2,
 \qquad P(R-PR)^2\leq PR^2\leq v_{T,\Delta}.
\]
Moreover, for every integer \(j\geq2\),
\[
 P|R-PR|^j\leq2^{j-2}P(R-PR)^2.
\]
Expanding the exponential series and applying exponential Markov inequality therefore gives the Bernstein bound
\[
 P\left\{|U_{a,\Delta}-PU_{a,\Delta}|>
 \sqrt{\frac{2v_{T,\Delta}x}{J_a}}+\frac{4x}{3J_a}\right\}
 \leq2e^{-x}. \tag{4}
\]
The displayed linear term is conservative relative to the value obtained by direct optimization.  Taking \(x=x_\eta=\log(6/\eta)\), the union of the exceptional events in (3) and the two instances of (4) has probability at most \(\eta\).  On its complement, (1), the triangle inequality, and \(|b_{T,\Delta}|\leq B_{T,\Delta}\) imply \(\tau\in I_{T,\Delta}^{\mathrm{conc}}\) whenever \(E_T\) occurs.  Since \(\tau\in[-2,2]\), intersection with \([-2,2]\) cannot remove the target, and on \(E_T^c\) the reported interval is \([-2,2]\).  Consequently this coverage argument is unconditional and does not condition on quota success.

It remains to validate the Gaussian branch and the observable splice.  Define
\[
 V_T=\sigma_{1,T}^2+\mathbf 1\{\alpha=0\}\sigma_{0,T}^2.
\]
Consider first an arbitrary triangular sequence of laws for which \(V_T\geq1/\log T\).  When \(\alpha>0\),
\[
 s_{T,\Delta}^2\geq\frac{1}{K_1\log T};
\]
when \(\alpha=0\), the quota orders in \(\mathrm{lem:quota\text{-}success}\) give \(s_{T,\Delta}^2\geq c_0/(T\log T)\) for a constant \(c_0>0\).  Express \(Z_T/s_{T,\Delta}=\sum_j\xi_{Tj}\) as the sum of its independent centered tape summands.  Their variances sum to one.  Bounded outcomes and the preceding variance lower bounds give
\[
 \delta_T^*:=\max_j|\xi_{Tj}|
 =O\left(\sqrt{\frac{\log T}{K_1}}\right)=o(1)
 \quad(\alpha>0),
\]
and \(\delta_T^*=O(\sqrt{\log T/T})=o(1)\) when \(\alpha=0\).  These bounds are uniform over the stated variance regime because \(K_1\asymp T^{1-\alpha}\).

For fixed real \(u\), Taylor's formula with \(|\xi_{Tj}|\leq\delta_T^*\) gives
\[
 P e^{iu\xi_{Tj}}
 =1-\frac{u^2}{2}P\xi_{Tj}^2
 +O\bigl(|u|^3\delta_T^*P\xi_{Tj}^2\bigr).
\]
Also
\[
 \sum_j(P\xi_{Tj}^2)^2
 \leq (\delta_T^*)^2\sum_jP\xi_{Tj}^2=(\delta_T^*)^2.
\]
Taking logarithms and summing proves
\[
 P\exp\{iuZ_T/s_{T,\Delta}\}=\exp\{-u^2/2+o(1)\}. \tag{5}
\]
The error is uniform.  The unit second moment gives tightness, and (5) identifies every subsequential limit as standard normal.  A contradiction-subsequence argument, using continuity of the Gaussian distribution function, therefore yields
\[
 \sup_{(P,\Pi,T):,V_T\geq1/\log T}\sup_{x\in\mathbb R}
 \left|P\{Z_T/s_{T,\Delta}\leq x\}-\Phi(x)\right|\longrightarrow0. \tag{6}
\]
This derives the Gaussian limit from bounded summands and the deterministic quota orders; no limit of \(t^\alpha\pi_t(1)\) is used.

The correction need not be independent of \(Z_T\).  The variance bound in \(\mathrm{lem:old\text{-}cohort\text{-}correction}\) and the quota orders give
\[
 PC_T^2=O\bigl(T^{-\rho(\beta+1-\alpha)}\bigr).
\]
In both cases \(\alpha>0\) and \(\alpha=0\), the variance lower bound above implies
\[
 \frac{PC_T^2}{s_{T,\Delta}^2}
 \leq C_1(\log T)T^{1-\alpha-\rho(\beta+1-\alpha)}\longrightarrow0, \tag{7}
\]
because \(\rho(\beta+1-\alpha)>1-\alpha\).

For a sample of size \(K\geq2\), the usual sample variance is
\[
 \widehat\sigma^2=\frac{K}{K-1}\{\overline{X^2}-\bar X^2\}.
\]
Since \(|X|\leq1\), Chebyshev's inequality applied to \(\overline{X^2}\) and \(\bar X\) gives, uniformly in the tape law,
\[
 \widehat\sigma_{X,a,\Delta}^2-\sigma_{a,T}^2=O_P(K_a^{-1/2}). \tag{8}
\]
When \(\alpha>0\), division by \(s_{T,\Delta}^2\geq1/(K_1\log T)\) bounds the relative arm-one error by
\[
 O_P(\log T/\sqrt{K_1})=o_P(1),
\]
and the arm-zero error by
\[
 O_P(K_1\log T/K_0^{3/2})=o_P(1).
\]
When \(\alpha=0\), both quotas are comparable to \(T\), and division by \(c_0/(T\log T)\) gives the same conclusion.  Hence
\[
 \widehat s_{T,\Delta}/s_{T,\Delta}\longrightarrow1 \tag{9}
\]
uniformly on \(V_T\geq1/\log T\).  Equations (1), (6), (7), and (9), together with \(P(E_T^c)\leq4T^{-4}\), imply the uniform studentized approximation on this regime.  Assigning the quotient the value zero on \(E_T^c\) changes its distribution function by at most \(P(E_T^c)\).

The regular class eventually lies in this high-variance regime.  Indeed, for \(X=Y\mathbf 1\{D\leq g_{T,\Delta}\}\), boundedness gives
\[
 \begin{aligned}
 |\operatorname{Var}(X)-\operatorname{Var}(Y)|
 &\leq |P(X^2-Y^2)|+|(PX)^2-(PY)^2|\\
 &\leq3P\{D>g_{T,\Delta}\}
 \leq3v_{T,\Delta}. 
 \end{aligned} \tag{10}
\]
Since \(g_{T,\Delta}\geq m_T\to\infty\), the right side tends to zero uniformly.  The regular-variance assumption thus gives \(V_T\geq\kappa/2\) eventually, also when \(\alpha=0\) after adding the two bounds in (10).  This proves both studentization assertions over \(\mathfrak M_{T,\Delta}^{\mathrm{reg}}(\kappa)\).

We now prove coverage for the Gaussian radius.  Put
\[
 f_B(s)=s c_\eta(B/s),\qquad s>0.
\]
If \(Z\) is standard normal, the defining equation for \(c_\eta\) and monotonicity in the magnitude of the shift imply, for every \(|b|\leq B\),
\[
 P\{|sZ-b|\leq f_B(s)\}
 =\Phi(c_\eta(B/s)+b/s)+\Phi(c_\eta(B/s)-b/s)-1
 \geq1-\eta. \tag{11}
\]
Let \(u=B/s\) and \(x=c_\eta(u)-u\).  The defining equation implies
\[
 z_{1-\eta}\leq x\leq z_{1-\eta/2},
 \qquad
 B+z_{1-\eta}s\leq f_B(s)\leq B+z_{1-\eta/2}s. \tag{12}
\]
Implicit differentiation gives
\[
 c_\eta'(u)=
 \frac{\phi(c_\eta(u)-u)-\phi(c_\eta(u)+u)}
 {\phi(c_\eta(u)-u)+\phi(c_\eta(u)+u)}\in[0,1]
\]
and therefore
\[
 f_B'(s)=x+
 \frac{2u\phi(x+2u)}{\phi(x)+\phi(x+2u)}.
\]
This derivative is bounded uniformly in \(B\geq0\) and \(s>0\): use \(x\geq z_{1-\eta}>0\) and
\[
 \frac{\phi(x+2u)}{\phi(x)}=\exp\{-2ux-2u^2\}.
\]
Thus (9) implies \(f_{B_{T,\Delta}}(\widehat s_{T,\Delta})-f_{B_{T,\Delta}}(s_{T,\Delta})=o_P(s_{T,\Delta})\), uniformly on the high-variance regime.  Combining this Lipschitz bound, (11), and the uniform Kolmogorov approximation already proved shows that
\[
 \inf_{(P,\Pi,T):,V_T\geq1/\log T}
 P\{\tau\in I_{T,\Delta}^{\mathrm G}\}\geq1-\eta-o(1). \tag{13}
\]
For completeness, this last implication follows by shrinking the deterministic interval in (11) by \(\epsilon s_{T,\Delta}\), paying at most \(2\epsilon/\sqrt{2\pi}\) under the Gaussian law, then using (6)--(9), and finally letting \(\epsilon\downarrow0\).  The nonnegative term \(d_{T,\Delta}\) can only enlarge the interval.

The quota orders and the two strict inequalities imposed on \(\rho\) give
\[
 d_{T,\Delta}
 =O\left(
 \sqrt{T^{-\rho(\beta+1-\alpha)}\log T}
 +T^{-\rho(1-\alpha)}\log T\right)
 =o(T^{-(1-\alpha)/2}). \tag{14}
\]
It remains to check the data-dependent splice.  If \(V_T\leq1/\log T\), (8) and Chebyshev's inequality imply
\[
 \sup_{(P,\Pi,T):,V_T\leq1/\log T}P(G_{T,\Delta})
 \leq C_2(\log T)^2/K_1\longrightarrow0. \tag{15}
\]
Indeed, gate success requires the relevant sample-variance sum to exceed its population counterpart by at least \(1/\log T\).  Hence in this regime the selected interval equals the concentration interval except on an event of probability \(o(1)\).

If \(V_T>1/\log T\), then on \(G_{T,\Delta}^c\), the deterministic gate inequality and the bound \(\widehat\sigma^2\leq2\) imply
\[
 \widehat s_{T,\Delta}^2
 \leq \frac{2}{K_1\log T}+\frac{2}{K_0}
 =o(T^{-(1-\alpha)})
 \quad(\alpha>0),
\]
whereas \(\widehat s_{T,\Delta}^2=O(1/(T\log T))\) when \(\alpha=0\).  Thus \(\widehat s_{T,\Delta}=o(T^{-(1-\alpha)/2})\) uniformly on gate failure.  Moreover
\[
 a_T=\sqrt{2S_Tx_\eta}\asymp T^{-(1-\alpha)/2}.
\]
By (12) and (14), for all sufficiently large \(T\),
\[
 f_{B_{T,\Delta}}(\widehat s_{T,\Delta})+d_{T,\Delta}
 \leq B_{T,\Delta}+a_T.
\]
The concentration radius is at least \(B_{T,\Delta}+a_T\).  Therefore, on gate failure the concentration interval contains the Gaussian interval; on gate success the selected interval is the Gaussian interval.  By (13), the selected interval is uniformly honest in the high-variance regime.  By (3)--(4) and (15), it is uniformly honest in the low-variance regime.  The full interval on \(E_T^c\) completes the proof over both declared model classes, without conditioning on quota success or assuming convergence of the scaled propensity.

The proposition is the upper-bound part of \(\mathrm{thm:one\text{-}sided\text{-}minimax\text{-}length\text{-}frontier}\), applied to exactly \(\mathfrak M_T^{\mathrm{low}}(\alpha,\beta,L,c,\varepsilon)\) and to the same deterministic quotas and hybrid interval.  That theorem gives
\[
 \inf_{(P,\Pi,T)\in\mathfrak M_T^{\mathrm{low}}}
 P\{\tau\in I_{T,\Delta}\}\geq1-\eta-o(1)
\]
and
\[
 \sup_{(P,\Pi,T)\in\mathfrak M_T^{\mathrm{low}}}
 \mathbb E_{P,\Pi}|I_{T,\Delta}|
 \leq C_\eta r_{T,\Delta}.
\]
These are precisely uniform honesty and the claimed expected-length bound.  The proof of the theorem shows explicitly that the construction uses only the arm-one lower allocation envelope and the control-arm floor through the deterministic quota orders; no upper allocation envelope is invoked.

Bounded outcomes imply \(\operatorname{Var}_P\{Y(a)\}\leq1\).  Hence nonemptiness of \(\mathfrak M_{T,\Delta}^{\mathrm{reg}}(\kappa)\) requires \(\kappa\leq1\) when \(\alpha>0\) and \(\kappa\leq2\) when \(\alpha=0\).  Conversely, under either displayed restriction, take prompt symmetric Rademacher outcomes in both arms, zero delays, and the deterministic policy \(\pi_t(1)=ct^{-\alpha}\).  It satisfies the one-sided exploration condition, and \(\pi_t(0)=1-ct^{-\alpha}\geq1-c\geq\varepsilon\); thus the stated restrictions are also sufficient.

On this regular class, (10) in the proof of \(\mathrm{thm:uniform\text{-}gated\text{-}inference}\), the regular-variance condition, and the deterministic quota orders imply constants \(0<c_0<C_0<\infty\) such that
\[
 c_0T^{-(1-\alpha)}\leq s_{T,\Delta}^2
 \leq C_0T^{-(1-\alpha)}. \tag{16}
\]
The upper bound uses \(\sigma_{a,T}^2\leq1\); for the lower bound, arm one alone suffices when \(\alpha>0\), while both quotas are comparable to \(T\) when \(\alpha=0\).  The studentized theorem and \(\mathrm{lem:old\text{-}cohort\text{-}correction}\) give
\[
 \frac{\widehat\tau_{T,\Delta}-\tau}{\widehat s_{T,\Delta}}
 =\frac{\widehat\tau_{T,\Delta}-\tau+b_{T,\Delta}}
 {\widehat s_{T,\Delta}}
 -\frac{b_{T,\Delta}}{\widehat s_{T,\Delta}}, \tag{17}
\]
and
\[
 \sup_{\mathfrak M_{T,\Delta}^{\mathrm{reg}}(\kappa)}
 \frac{|b_{T,\Delta}|}{s_{T,\Delta}}
 \leq C_1T^{(1-\alpha)/2}(1+T+\Delta_T)^{-\beta}. \tag{18}
\]
If the right side tends to zero, variance consistency makes the second term in (17) uniformly \(o_P(1)\), while the first term is uniformly standard normal.  The ordinary \(z_{1-\eta/2}\) interval is therefore uniformly asymptotically honest.

For necessity, construct an explicit compatible triangular family.  Put
\[
 \delta_T=\min\{1/4,L(1+H_T)^{-\beta}\}.
\]
Fix \(\gamma\in\{-1,1\}\), let \(s_1=\gamma\) and \(s_0=-\gamma\), and use the deterministic policy \(\pi_t(1)=ct^{-\alpha}\).  Independently over arrivals and arms, with probability \(\delta_T\) set
\[
 (D_t(a),Y_t(a))=(H_T+1,s_a),
\]
and with probability \(1-\delta_T\) set \(D_t(a)=0\) and draw \(Y_t(a)\in\{-1,1\}\) with mean
\[
 -\frac{\delta_Ts_a}{1-\delta_T}.
\]
The mean is admissible because \(\delta_T\leq1/4\).  The delay-tail calculation is
\[
 P\{D_t(a)>u\}=
 \begin{cases}
  \delta_T,&0\leq u\leq H_T,\\
  0,&u\geq H_T+1,
 \end{cases}
 \leq\min\{1,L(1+u)^{-\beta}\}. \tag{19}
\]
All outcomes are bounded and every delay is finite.  Furthermore,
\[
 PY_t(a)=\delta_Ts_a+(1-\delta_T)
 \left(-\frac{\delta_Ts_a}{1-\delta_T}\right)=0,
 \qquad \operatorname{Var}_P\{Y_t(a)\}=1. \tag{20}
\]
Thus the construction belongs to every support-feasible regular class.  Since \(g_{T,\Delta}<h_{T,\Delta}<H_T+1\), its correction variables vanish, whereas
\[
 b_{T,\Delta}=2\gamma\delta_T. \tag{21}
\]
The visible variables have variance \(1-\delta_T-\delta_T^2\to1\).  Integral comparison in the quota definition gives
\[
 T^{1-\alpha}/K_1(n_T)\longrightarrow(1-\alpha)/c,
\]
and, when \(\alpha=0\), also \(T/K_0(n_T)\to1/\varepsilon\).  Consequently, for some \(s_*>0\),
\[
 T^{(1-\alpha)/2}s_{T,\Delta}\longrightarrow s_*. \tag{22}
\]
The centered studentized term in (17) converges to \(N(0,1)\), while (21)--(22) show
\[
 \frac{b_{T,\Delta}}{s_{T,\Delta}}
 =\frac{2\gamma L}{s_*}
 T^{(1-\alpha)/2}(1+H_T)^{-\beta}(1+o(1)). \tag{23}
\]
If the product in (23) converges to a finite positive constant, choose \(\gamma=1\); then (17) converges to \(N(-u,1)\) for some \(u>0\).  Its ordinary-Wald coverage converges to
\[
 \Phi(z_{1-\eta/2}-u)+\Phi(z_{1-\eta/2}+u)-1<1-\eta. \tag{24}
\]
If the product diverges, the centered term remains tight while the absolute shift diverges, so coverage tends to zero.  Truncation by \([-2,2]\) is asymptotically inactive because both \(\delta_T\) and \(s_{T,\Delta}\) tend to zero.  If the product merely fails to tend to zero, select a subsequence on which it is bounded away from zero and then a further subsequence on which it either has a positive finite limit or diverges.  Thus uniform honesty is impossible unless the product tends to zero.  This proves the equivalence.

Finally, when \(\Delta_T=0\),
\[
 T^{(1-\alpha)/2}(1+T)^{-\beta}
 =T^{(1-\alpha)/2-\beta}(1+o(1)),
\]
which tends to zero exactly when \(\beta>(1-\alpha)/2\).

A stationary binary endpoint lies in \([0,1]\subset[-1,1]\), and its armwise risk difference is exactly the causal contrast \(\tau=PY(1)-PY(0)\).  The logged two-sided rare-arm envelope implies the one-sided arm-one exploration floor; because there are two arms and \(C\leq1-\varepsilon\), it also gives
\[
 \pi_t(0)=1-\pi_t(1)\geq1-Ct^{-\alpha}\geq1-C\geq\varepsilon. \tag{25}
\]
Thus a trial satisfying the stated sampling, randomization, and delay conditions is covered by the preceding inference results.

The necessity is genuinely class-wide and is also available with binary outcomes.  In the construction used for the Wald converse, replace the Rademacher outcomes as follows.  With probability \(\delta_T\), delay the endpoint to \(H_T+1\), assigning hidden values \((1,0)\) to arms \((1,0)\) for one sign and \((0,1)\) for the other.  With probability \(1-\delta_T\), reveal the endpoint immediately and draw a Bernoulli variable in arm \(a\) with mean
\[
 \frac{1/2-\delta_TH_a}{1-\delta_T},
\]
where \(H_a\in\{0,1\}\) is that arm's hidden value.  Since \(\delta_T\leq1/4\), these probabilities lie in \([0,1]\).  Each eventual arm mean is \(1/2\), each eventual variance is \(1/4\), the visible contrast is the negative of the hidden contrast, and the absolute hidden bias is \(\delta_T\).  The tail calculation (19) is unchanged.  Hence whenever
\[
 T^q(1+T+\Delta_T)^{-\beta}\not\longrightarrow0,
\]
this binary subfamily yields either a nonzero shifted-Gaussian limit or a diverging shift, and disproves uniform honesty of the unpadded Wald interval.  This argument asserts no failure at every individual law.

If the regular-variance condition is independently verified, the sufficiency half of \(\mathrm{prop:wald\text{-}followup\text{-}frontier}\) shows that the displayed product tending to zero suffices for ordinary Wald.  Without regular variance, \(\mathrm{thm:uniform\text{-}gated\text{-}inference}\) supplies the bias-aware Gaussian branch only behind the observable variance gate and otherwise supplies the concentration branch; the concentration branch alone is also valid by its finite-sample argument.  Therefore the stated pad, fallback, or additional-follow-up choices follow from the same terminal records and do not silently impose a nondegenerate Gaussian approximation.

It remains to solve the follow-up inequality.  Since \(q=(1-\alpha)/2>0\), no additional follow-up is needed when \(\beta>q\), because
\[
 T^q(1+T)^{-\beta}\longrightarrow0.
\]
When \(\beta=q\),
\[
 T^q(1+T+\Delta_T)^{-q}\longrightarrow0
 \quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad
 \Delta_T/T\longrightarrow\infty. \tag{26}
\]
When \(\beta<q\), raising the positive quantities to the power \(1/\beta\) gives
\[
 T^q(1+T+\Delta_T)^{-\beta}\longrightarrow0
 \quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad
 T+\Delta_T\gg T^{q/\beta}. \tag{27}
\]
At a particular prompt-delay law, \(b_{T,\Delta}=0\); thus the uniform obstruction is compatible with pointwise ordinary-Wald validity at such a law.

Put \(q=(1-\alpha)/2\).  We first compare the design classes.  If \((P,\Pi,T)\in\mathfrak M_T(\alpha,\beta,L,c,C,\varepsilon)\), then the two-sided rare-arm condition gives \(\pi_t(1)\geq ct^{-\alpha}\), and, because there are two arms,
\[
 \pi_t(0)=1-\pi_t(1)\geq1-Ct^{-\alpha}\geq1-C\geq\varepsilon. \tag{28}
\]
All remaining defining assumptions are shared, so
\[
 \mathfrak M_T(\alpha,\beta,L,c,C,\varepsilon)
 \subseteq\mathfrak M_T^{\mathrm{low}}(\alpha,\beta,L,c,\varepsilon). \tag{29}
\]
In particular, the fixed policy
\[
 p_t:=\pi_t(1)=ct^{-\alpha},
 \qquad \pi_t(0)=1-p_t, \tag{30}
\]
belongs to the one-sided class because \(1-p_t\geq1-c\geq\varepsilon\).  It also belongs to the contained two-sided class because \(c\leq C\).

\emph{Upper bound.}
Uniform coverage is \(\mathrm{thm:uniform\text{-}gated\text{-}inference}\).  To bound length, let
\[
 S_T=K_1(n_T)^{-1}+K_0(n_T)^{-1}.
\]
By \(\mathrm{lem:quota\text{-}success}\), uniformly over the one-sided class,
\[
 K_1(n_T)\asymp T^{1-\alpha},\quad K_0(n_T)\asymp T,
 \quad J_1\asymp T^{\rho(1-\alpha)},\quad J_0\asymp T^\rho. \tag{31}
\]
It follows that
\[
 S_T=O(T^{-(1-\alpha)}),
 \qquad a_T=\sqrt{2S_Tx_\eta}=O(T^{-q}). \tag{32}
\]
Because \(g_{T,\Delta}=m_T+\Delta_T\geq m_T\asymp T^\rho\), the delay envelope gives
\[
 v_{T,\Delta}=O(T^{-\rho\beta}). \tag{33}
\]
For every fixed \(x>0\), (31)--(33) imply
\[
 \begin{aligned}
 A_{1,T,\Delta}(x)
 &=O\left(T^{-\rho(\beta+1-\alpha)/2}
       +T^{-\rho(1-\alpha)}\right)=o(T^{-q}),\\
 A_{0,T,\Delta}(x)
 &=O\left(T^{-\rho(\beta+1)/2}+T^{-\rho}\right)=o(T^{-q}).
 \end{aligned} \tag{34}
\]
The first line uses \(\rho(\beta+1-\alpha)>1-\alpha\) and \(\rho>1/2\); the arm-zero exponents are larger.  The strict inequalities also absorb logarithms, so
\[
 d_{T,\Delta}=o(T^{-q}). \tag{35}
\]

For observations in \([-1,1]\), the usual sample variance is at most two.  Hence, on \(E_T\),
\[
 \widehat s_{T,\Delta}^2\leq2S_T,
 \qquad \widehat s_{T,\Delta}=O(T^{-q}). \tag{36}
\]
Let \(z=z_{1-\eta/2}\).  Evaluating the defining coverage function of \(c_\eta(u)\) at \(u+z\) gives
\[
 \Phi(z)+\Phi(2u+z)-1\geq2\Phi(z)-1=1-\eta.
\]
Since that function is increasing in its critical-value argument,
\[
 c_\eta(u)\leq u+z,
 \qquad
 \widehat s_{T,\Delta}c_\eta(B_{T,\Delta}/\widehat s_{T,\Delta})
 \leq B_{T,\Delta}+z\widehat s_{T,\Delta}. \tag{37}
\]
The zero-standard-error convention is already part of the interval definition.

Next, \(h_{T,\Delta}=H_T-k_T\), \(H_T\geq T\), and \(k_T=O(T^\rho)\) with \(\rho<1\), so
\[
 \frac{1+h_{T,\Delta}}{1+H_T}
 =1-\frac{k_T}{1+H_T}=1+o(1) \tag{38}
\]
uniformly over deterministic \(\Delta_T\geq0\).  Therefore
\[
 B_{T,\Delta}=O((1+H_T)^{-\beta}). \tag{39}
\]
Equations (32), (34), and (39) bound the concentration-branch length by a constant multiple of \(r_{T,\Delta}\).  Equations (35)--(37) and (39) give the same bound for the Gaussian branch.  Intersecting with \([-2,2]\) cannot increase length.  On \(E_T^c\), the interval has length four, while
\[
 4P(E_T^c)\leq16T^{-4}=o(T^{-q})=o(r_{T,\Delta}) \tag{40}
\]
by \(\mathrm{lem:quota\text{-}success}\).  Taking expectations proves the asserted uniform upper bound.

\emph{Sampling converse.}
Use the single policy (30), set both delays to zero, and set \(Y_t(0)=0\).  In arm one define independent and identically distributed laws \(P_+\) and \(P_-\) by
\[
 P_+\{Y_t(1)=1\}=P_-\{Y_t(1)=-1\}=\frac{1+d_T}{2},
 \qquad d_T=\lambda Q_T^{-1/2},
 \qquad Q_T=\sum_{t=1}^Tp_t, \tag{41}
\]
with complementary probabilities on the other Rademacher value.  Choose
\[
 0<\lambda<\frac{1-2\eta}{2\sqrt2}.
\]
Since \(\alpha<1\), integral comparison gives
\[
 Q_T\asymp T^{1-\alpha},
 \qquad d_T\asymp T^{-q}, \tag{42}
\]
and \(d_T<1\) eventually.  The two experiments satisfy every defining condition of the one-sided class, and their causal contrasts are \(\tau_+=d_T\) and \(\tau_-=-d_T\).

Assignments and logged propensities have the same law.  Conditional on assignment to arm zero, the observed record has the same law; conditional on arm one, the Hellinger affinity of the two Rademacher laws is \(\sqrt{1-d_T^2}\).  Independence over arrivals and the deterministic policy give the exact observed-experiment affinity
\[
 \begin{aligned}
 \operatorname{Aff}(P_+^O,P_-^O)
 &=\prod_{t=1}^T\left[1-p_t\{1-\sqrt{1-d_T^2}\}\right]\\
 &\geq1-\sum_{t=1}^Tp_td_T^2
 =1-\lambda^2. 
 \end{aligned} \tag{43}
\]
Here \(1-\sqrt{1-x}\leq x\) and \(\prod_t(1-x_t)\geq1-\sum_tx_t\) for arguments in \([0,1]\).  For two dominated laws with affinity \(A\), Cauchy--Schwarz gives
\[
 \|P-Q\|_{\mathrm{TV}}
 =\frac12\int|\sqrt p-\sqrt q|(\sqrt p+\sqrt q)
 \leq\sqrt{1-A^2}. \tag{44}
\]
Consequently,
\[
 \|P_+^O-P_-^O\|_{\mathrm{TV}}\leq\sqrt2\lambda. \tag{45}
\]

Let \(J_{T,\Delta}\) be uniformly honest on the one-sided class.  Under \(P_+^O\), the union bound and (45) give
\[
 P_+^O\{\tau_+\in J_{T,\Delta},\ \tau_-\in J_{T,\Delta}\}
 \geq1-2\eta-o(1)-\sqrt2\lambda. \tag{46}
\]
The right side is eventually bounded below by a positive constant.  On this event the interval has length at least \(2d_T\); hence
\[
 \sup_{(P,\Pi,T)\in\mathfrak M_T^{\mathrm{low}}}
 \mathbb E_{P,\Pi}|J_{T,\Delta}|
 \geq c_{\eta,1}T^{-q}. \tag{47}
\]

\emph{Hidden-tail converse.}
Retain (30) and set
\[
 \delta_T=\min\{1/4,L(1+H_T)^{-\beta}\}. \tag{48}
\]
For each arrival and arm, independently draw a Bernoulli indicator with success probability \(\delta_T\).  On failure set \((Y_t(a),D_t(a))=(0,0)\).  On success set \(D_t(a)=H_T+1\); under \(P_+\), use successful outcomes \(+1\) in arm one and \(-1\) in arm zero, and under \(P_-\) reverse both signs.  For every integer \(u\geq0\),
\[
 P_\pm\{D_t(a)>u\}
 =\begin{cases}
 \delta_T,&0\leq u\leq H_T,\\
 0,&u\geq H_T+1,
 \end{cases}
 \leq\min\{1,L(1+u)^{-\beta}\}. \tag{49}
\]
Thus both laws are in the one-sided class and all delays are finite.

No successful atom is revealed by \(H_T\).  The laws of the immediate zero records, absence indicators, assignments, logged propensities, and hence all of \(O_{T,\Delta}\), are identical under \(P_+\) and \(P_-\).  This uses no outcome--delay independence: the hidden sign is deliberately coupled to its delay.  The eventual causal contrasts nevertheless satisfy
\[
 \tau_+=2\delta_T,
 \qquad \tau_-=-2\delta_T. \tag{50}
\]
Under the common observed law, honesty and a union bound yield
\[
 P\{\tau_+\in J_{T,\Delta},\ \tau_-\in J_{T,\Delta}\}
 \geq1-2\eta-o(1). \tag{51}
\]
On this event \(|J_{T,\Delta}|\geq4\delta_T\).  Since \(H_T\geq T\to\infty\), (48) equals \(L(1+H_T)^{-\beta}\) eventually, and therefore
\[
 \sup_{(P,\Pi,T)\in\mathfrak M_T^{\mathrm{low}}}
 \mathbb E_{P,\Pi}|J_{T,\Delta}|
 \geq c_{\eta,2}(1+H_T)^{-\beta}. \tag{52}
\]
The affinity calculation (43) and the identical-law calculation before (50) are exact for every finite \(T\), including experiments with at most four assignments.  They therefore provide the requested smallest-instance stress test and do not condition on quota success or on recruitment stopping.  At the asymptotic boundary, \(\alpha<1\) ensures \(K_1\to\infty\), while the normalized maximum tape summand is \(o(1)\), as proved in (5); this checks the primitive Gaussian boundary rather than assuming it.

Combining (47) and (52), and using
\[
 \max\{c_{\eta,1}x,c_{\eta,2}y\}
 \geq\min\{c_{\eta,1},c_{\eta,2}\}\max\{x,y\},
\]
proves the lower bound at
\[
 r_{T,\Delta}=\max\{T^{-q},(1+H_T)^{-\beta}\}.
\]
Together with the upper bound this proves the exact class-minimax order.  When \(\Delta_T=0\), \(H_T=T\), giving \(\max\{T^{-(1-\alpha)/2},T^{-\beta}\}\).
